issues.legal_issue: The power to designate an area for redevelopment is not arbitrary or discriminatory when its scope is guided by the damage and redevelopment purpose the legislation addresses.
material_facts: The legislation was enacted to address extensive damage to buildings caused by serious communal rioting and to enable planned improvement of damaged urban areas.
The government declared the entire walled city of Amritsar to be a damaged area, and the challenged schemes concerned areas within it.
The petitioners argued that the definition gave the government no criteria and that the declaration was vague.
issues.conclusion: The designation power was not arbitrary, unguided or uncanalised, and the declaration was not vague; there was no violation of Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not invalidate a designation power where the legislation’s purpose and the circumstances it addresses guide its exercise. The Court relied on the purpose of the Punjab Development of Damaged Areas Act, 1951, and section 2(d), which permits declaration of an area as damaged, including areas already notified under the earlier legislation. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.redevelopment_purpose_guides_designation: The governing scheme addresses damaged urban areas through planned improvement.
predicates.designated_area_falls_within_the_affecte: The designated area lies within the area affected by the damage addressed by the scheme.

issues.definition: When an area is designated for a redevelopment purpose guided by serious urban damage and the designation falls within the affected area, the designation power is not arbitrary or vague.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory scheme does not create an arbitrary choice between acquisition regimes merely because it incorporates provisions of another redevelopment law.
material_facts: The petitioners argued that the Improvement Trust could choose between the challenged Act and the Punjab Town Improvement Act, with different compensation consequences.

The challenged Act allowed a scheme to provide for matters listed in section 28 of the Punjab Town Improvement Act and treated schemes already framed under that Act as schemes under the challenged Act.
The Court found that these provisions did not give the Trust a choice to acquire property under either law.
issues.conclusion: The Act gave no arbitrary discretion to choose between the two acquisition regimes; the Article 14 challenge on this ground failed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court read section 3 of the Punjab Development of Damaged Areas Act, 1951, as incorporating specified matters from section 28 of the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922, and deeming existing schemes under the latter to have been framed under the former. That arrangement did not establish an option to select either law. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.other_law_provisions_are_incorporated_fo: The governing framework uses provisions of another law to identify matters that a scheme may address.

predicates.no_choice_between_acquisition_regimes: The acquiring authority is not given an option to acquire the same property under either of two regimes.

issues.definition: When another law supplies scheme content or existing schemes are carried over, but the acquiring authority has no choice between acquisition regimes, the framework is not arbitrary on the basis of such a choice.

issues.legal_issue: Restrictions on property rights and the right to carry on business are reasonable when they serve planned improvement for the public and affected persons have meaningful opportunities to object and pursue review.
material_facts: The Act enabled planned improvement schemes for damaged areas of the city.
Affected persons could object to schemes before the Trust and the government considered them, participate in compensation inquiries, challenge specified matters before a Tribunal, and pursue appeals.
The Court noted that some buildings might be newly built or undamaged but found that this did not justify blocking a scheme serving a social purpose.
The Trust had assured displaced shop occupants that alternative accommodation or shops would be available, subject to the stated arrangements.
issues.conclusion: The restrictions were reasonable and served the general public; they were protected by Articles 19(5) and 19(6) and did not violate Article 19(1)(f) or Article 19(1)(g).
issues.legal_principle: The reasonableness of restrictions under Article 19 is assessed by balancing the nature of the right, the purpose of the restrictions, the urgency of the evil, and the necessity of remedying it against the social welfare purpose. Articles 19(5) and 19(6) permit reasonable restrictions in the interests identified there. The Court applied this test without citing an earlier case.

issues.definition: When a public-welfare redevelopment scheme allows objections and compensation review, and affected occupants receive alternative-accommodation assurances, the restrictions on property and business rights are reasonable.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for property acquired under a redevelopment scheme is not constitutionally inadequate or illusory when it includes a market-value floor and may share the scheme’s proceeds.
material_facts: Compensation was calculated by reference to the scheme’s income and costs, with the total distributed among persons according to their interests.

The legislation required that an interested person receive no less than the market value of that person’s interest, subject to demolition and removal costs, and separately provided compensation for structures.
The statutory definition of land was broad enough to include buildings.
The Trust had to submit the scheme statement within the prescribed statutory limit, and the scheme could produce compensation exceeding the market-value floor.
The petitioners objected that final compensation could be delayed and that interest was not payable during the delay.
issues.conclusion: The compensation was neither inadequate nor illusory and did not violate Article 31(2).
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as considered by the Court, was not violated where the statutory method provided at least the market value of the claimant’s interest, subject to specified deductions, and could yield more through sharing scheme proceeds. The Court relied on sections 11–13 and 16 of the Punjab Development of Damaged Areas Act, 1951, and the broad definition of land comparable to section 3(a) of the Land Acquisition Act. It also noted the statutory timetable for submitting the scheme statement. No earlier cases are cited.

issues.legal_issue: Acquisition for a planned redevelopment scheme serving a public or social purpose does not cease to be for a public purpose merely because public funds are not contributed.
material_facts: The petitioners argued that the acquisition was not for a public purpose because no government or local-authority funds were contributed.
The Act provided for planned improvement of damaged urban areas, and the Court characterized the schemes as serving the public good and a social purpose.
The compensation arrangement linked payments to scheme income and expenditure and afforded affected persons at least the market value of their interests, subject to specified deductions.
issues.conclusion: The public-purpose objection was not sustainable; the Court treated the schemes as serving the public good despite the asserted absence of government or local-authority contributions.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated planned improvement of damaged urban areas as a social purpose and public good. Its conclusion arose in considering the acquisition and compensation challenge under Article 31(2), and did not depend on a cited earlier case.
